description: New original literary Reading Comprehension sets: five realistic-fiction passages and one poem, six questions each (ELA-RC-137 to ELA-RC-172, passages RC-P107 to RC-P112). Each set runs global to local to inferential and includes one TEI (multi-select or drag and drop).

passages.title: Trial 2
passages.body:
In this story, an eighth grader presents her project at a middle school science fair in Queens, New York.

Trial 2

1 The gym at Hamilton Middle School smelled like floor wax and nervous people. On forty folding tables, tri-fold poster boards leaned open like books that wanted to be read. Lena Ortiz had spent three nights gluing hers together. In thick blue letters across the top, it asked, DOES MUSIC HELP PLANTS GROW?

2 The answer, according to the poster, was yes. Beneath the title, a bar graph climbed like a staircase: plants that heard no music, plants that heard pop songs, and plants that heard Mozart, each bar taller than the last. Lena had arranged three healthy bean plants in paper cups at the front of the table. They looked green and confident. She did not feel either.

3 What the poster did not show was the second trial. In March, Lena had run the whole experiment again to be sure, and the results had collapsed. The silent plants grew just as tall as the musical ones. Two of the Mozart plants wilted for no reason she could find. She had written every measurement in her green composition notebook, and then she had closed the notebook and slid it under the table, behind her backpack, where it sat now like a secret holding its breath.

4 "It's still true," her friend Danny had said when she told him. "You just had a bad week. Show the good trial." He had made it sound simple, the way people make everything sound simple when it is not their project.

5 The judges moved down the row in pairs, carrying clipboards. When they reached Lena's table, one of them, a tall woman with short gray hair and reading glasses on a beaded chain, introduced herself as Dr. Pruitt, a retired chemist. The other judge was called away.

6 Lena gave her speech. She had practiced it in the bathroom mirror until the words wore smooth grooves in her mouth. Hypothesis, materials, procedure, results. Dr. Pruitt listened without writing anything down, which was worse than if she had written a great deal.

7 "How many times did you run it?" Dr. Pruitt asked.

8 The gym seemed to get louder. Somewhere a baking-soda volcano erupted to scattered applause. Lena thought of Danny's advice. She thought of the bar graph, so tall and tidy. Then she thought of the notebook behind her backpack, and she found that she could not make her mouth say "once."

9 "Twice," she said. "The second time it didn't work." She pulled out the notebook and opened it to the March pages, where the numbers marched down the columns in her careful handwriting, refusing to agree with her poster.

10 She waited for Dr. Pruitt to frown. Instead, the judge leaned in so close that her glasses swung forward on their chain. "Now this is interesting," she said. "What changed between the trials?"

11 "Nothing," Lena said. Then she stopped. "Well, the windowsill. In March I moved them to the other side of the classroom because of the radiator." She heard herself say it, and something clicked, like a key finding its lock. "So maybe it wasn't the music at all. Maybe the first group was just warmer."

12 Dr. Pruitt smiled for the first time. "Do you know how many experiments I ran in forty years that did exactly what I hoped the first time?" She held up a hand and made a zero with her fingers. "The surprises are where the science is. A result that disagrees with you is not a failure. It is information."

13 After the judges moved on, Lena looked at her poster for a long moment. Then she took a marker from her backpack and, beneath the bar graph, in letters smaller than the title but just as blue, she wrote: TRIAL 2: SEE NOTEBOOK. NEW QUESTION: WAS IT THE HEAT?

14 She did not win a ribbon that afternoon. But on the subway home, with the notebook open across her knees, she began sketching a third trial, one with a thermometer beside every cup.

passages.title: The Doorframe
passages.body:
In this story, a boy named Tomás and his family are packing to move out of the Brooklyn apartment where he has lived his whole life.

The Doorframe

1 By Saturday morning the apartment had stopped looking like a home and started looking like a warehouse. Cardboard towers rose in every room, each labeled in my mother's square capitals: KITCHEN (FRAGILE), BOOKS, TOMÁS (WINTER). Our voices bounced off walls that had been stripped of photographs, and the rooms sounded larger and emptier than I had ever heard them, as if the apartment were already forgetting us.

2 I had decided not to help. It was the only protest I had left. For two months I had argued against the move to my aunt's building in New Jersey: my school was here, my friends were here, the man at the bodega who saved me the last sesame bagel was here. My parents listened, nodded, and signed the lease anyway. So I sat on the radiator with my headphones on and watched everyone else work.

3 My father packed the way he did everything, quickly and without comment. He wrapped plates in newspaper, taped boxes shut with one long screech of tape, and whistled under his breath. Watching him made me angrier. He didn't seem to care at all that we were leaving the only place I could remember.

4 Around noon my mother tapped my shoulder and pointed to the kitchen doorway. "The landlord's painting next week," she said. "If you want anything from that, now's the time."

5 I knew what she meant without looking. On the left side of the doorframe, a ladder of pencil lines climbed from knee height to just below my shoulder. Each one had a date beside it and the letter T. My father had started them when I was two, standing me against the wood every September and laying a cereal box flat on my head to make the line straight.

6 You cannot pack a doorframe. I stood in front of it with my hands in my pockets and felt something hot rise in my throat. In a week, a stranger with a roller would erase eleven years in a few strokes.

7 Then my father was beside me, holding a roll of brown packing paper and a pencil. He didn't say anything. He tore off a long strip, held it flat against the wood, and nodded for me to trace. I pressed the pencil against the paper and found each groove by feel, the way you find a light switch in the dark. Age two. Age five, the year I broke my arm. Age nine, a sudden leap of three inches that my mother had called "the beanstalk year."

8 Near the bottom of the frame, below my earliest line, I found marks I had never noticed. They were older and fainter, and beside them, in handwriting I recognized as my grandmother's, were the letters R.M.

9 "Rafael Morales," my father said quietly. "This was her apartment before it was ours. I grew up in that kitchen."

10 I looked up at him. I had always known that, in the way you know facts about your parents without ever really thinking about them. But I had never pictured him small enough to stand against this frame. His jaw was tight. For the first time all morning, he wasn't whistling.

11 "You didn't say anything," I said. "All this time. You acted like it was nothing."

12 He shrugged, but it was a slow shrug, heavier than usual. "Somebody had to keep taping boxes," he said. "If I stopped, I wasn't sure I'd start again."

13 We traced his marks too, onto the same strip of paper, his faint lines below my dark ones, like the roots of a plant beneath its stem. When we finished, he rolled the paper carefully and handed it to me. "Your job," he said. "Don't let it get crushed."

14 I carried that roll down three flights of stairs myself, holding it upright in both hands the way you would carry a lit candle. Then I went back up and started taping boxes.

passages.title: First Board
passages.body:
In this story, an eighth grader on her school's chess team loses her top position to a younger player.

First Board

1 For two years, Nadia Haddad had sat at first board. On the chess team at her middle school in Brooklyn, that meant the first table, the hardest opponent, and the clock that everyone watched. She liked the weight of it. Before every match she lined up her pieces so that each knight faced exactly forward, as if they were soldiers waiting for inspection.

2 Then Owen Park arrived in sixth grade, small and loud and wearing a sweatshirt with a cartoon dinosaur on it. In his first week he beat three seventh graders. In his third week he beat Nadia, in a game so fast and so strange that she spent the whole subway ride home replaying it on her phone, trying to find the moment it had gone wrong.

3 Coach Bekele posted the new lineup on the classroom door the following Monday. OWEN PARK, BOARD 1. NADIA HADDAD, BOARD 2. Nadia read it twice, as though the letters might rearrange themselves if she stared hard enough. They did not.

4 "It's just a list," her friend Kezia said.

5 "It's not just a list," Nadia said. She did not explain, because she did not know how to say that first board had become a kind of address, the place where she lived.

6 It got worse. The next week, Coach Bekele handed her a folder of Owen's tournament games. "You're my best analyst," he said. "Figure out his weaknesses before the city finals. Other schools will be studying him, and I want us to know first."

7 Nadia took the folder home and spread the score sheets across her bedroom floor. She expected to find sloppiness. Owen played fast, and fast players made mistakes. At first she found plenty of them: a bishop left unprotected here, a pawn pushed too far there. She circled each one in red with grim satisfaction.

8 But as the evening went on, she noticed something else. Owen's mistakes did not seem to bother him. After losing a piece, he did not retreat into a shell and defend. He attacked. He sent his queen into the middle of the board and dared his opponents to deal with it, and more often than not they flinched. His losses were spectacular, but so were his wins, and there were many more wins.

9 Nadia sat back against her bed. She thought of her own games: the careful walls of pawns, the knights tucked safely at home, the draws she had accepted when she was ahead because a draw could not hurt her ranking. She had always called it discipline. Looking at Owen's games, scattered and fearless across the carpet, she began to suspect it had another name.

10 She did not sleep well. In the morning she brought the folder back with two pages of notes. The first page listed Owen's weaknesses, as she had been asked. The second page was titled, in her neatest handwriting, WHAT I SHOULD STEAL.

11 Coach Bekele read both pages without speaking. Then he looked at her over the top of the paper. "This second page," he said. "That's the most useful thing anyone's given me all year."

12 At practice that afternoon, Nadia sat down across from Owen. He grinned at her and bounced a pawn in his palm like a coin he was about to flip.

13 "Rematch?" he asked.

14 "Not exactly," she said. "I want you to show me what you were thinking in your game against Lefferts Academy. Move nine. The queen." She paused. "And I'll show you why you shouldn't have left your bishop alone on move six."

15 Owen considered this with great seriousness, then nodded. They bent over the board together, and for the next hour, the question of who sat at first board seemed to Nadia like a much smaller question than it had been on Monday. It was still there. It still mattered. But it had shrunk to the size of a single square, and the rest of the board was wide open.

passages.title: The Ferry Story
passages.body:
In this story, a girl records her grandmother's favorite story for a school project. "Lola" is a Filipino word for grandmother.

The Ferry Story

1 Every Thanksgiving, after the pie and before the dishes, my grandmother told the ferry story. My cousins and I could recite it along with her, and when we were younger, we sometimes did, which made Lola pretend to be offended.

2 The story went like this. In 1971, Lola arrived in New York from Manila with one suitcase and eleven dollars. On her first morning, she rode the Staten Island Ferry, because it was the only thing in the city she could afford. Halfway across the harbor, the Statue of Liberty appeared out of the fog, and a stranger, an old man in a fishing cap, turned to her and said, "Well. You made it." That was the whole story. It did not have an ending, exactly, but Lola always told it as though it did.

3 So when Ms. Adeyemi assigned an oral history project, I chose Lola because it seemed easy. I already knew the story. All I had to do was record it, type it up, and add a few paragraphs about immigration in the 1970s.

4 I set my phone on the kitchen table between us. Lola folded her hands and told the story, and I listened with half my attention, already planning my introduction.

5 That night, typing up the recording, I noticed the problem. In this version, the morning was not foggy. It was "bright, so bright the water hurt my eyes." She had not had eleven dollars, but "four dollars and a bus token." And the old man in the fishing cap had become a woman with a baby, who said, "Welcome home."

6 I played it back three times. Then I found a video my uncle had taken at Thanksgiving two years ago. Fog. Eleven dollars. Fishing cap. "Well. You made it."

7 My stomach sank. My whole project depended on the story being true, and now I had two stories, and they could not both be. I imagined someone in class asking which version was real, and me standing there with nothing to say.

8 The next afternoon I sat across from Lola again, without the phone. "Your story changed," I said. I tried to say it gently, but it came out sounding like an accusation.

9 She did not look surprised. She poured two cups of tea. "Of course it did," she said. "Who was I telling it to?"

10 I didn't understand, and she could see that. "At Thanksgiving," she said, "I tell it to your uncles, who worry too much about money. So there is very little money, and an old man who tells me I made it, because making it is what they need to hear about. Yesterday I told it to you. You are starting high school in the fall. You are nervous, though you don't say so. So I gave you a bright morning and a woman who said welcome."

11 "But which one really happened?" I asked.

12 Lola smiled the way she did when one of us lost at cards and didn't yet know why. "Both," she said. "Neither. I was nineteen and frightened, and I don't remember the weather. What I remember is that someone on that boat was kind to me, and that I decided, right there in the middle of the water, that I would stay."

13 I sat with that for a long time. The tea went cold between my hands.

14 In the end, I typed up both versions and set them side by side. Underneath, where my paragraphs about the 1970s were supposed to go, I wrote about a story that bends to fit whoever is listening, the way a river bends to fit its banks without ever stopping being a river. Ms. Adeyemi gave me an A, but that was not the part I kept thinking about. I kept thinking about the bright water, and the woman with the baby, and the fact that my grandmother had known I was nervous before I told anyone.

passages.title: What Hurry Costs
passages.body:
In this story, a teenager spends the summer as an apprentice in a furniture maker's shop in the Bronx.

What Hurry Costs

1 For the first three weeks of my apprenticeship, Mr. Albescu did not let me cut a single board. I swept. I sorted screws into coffee cans by size. Mostly, I sanded. He would hand me a plank and a block wrapped in sandpaper, say, "Until it feels like the inside of your wrist," and walk away.

2 The shop on Webster Avenue smelled of sawdust and linseed oil and the coffee Mr. Albescu brewed so strong it could have stripped paint. Along the back wall hung his tools, each in its own outline traced in black marker, so that an empty space shouted whenever something was missing. In the middle of the room stood the table saw, which I was not allowed to touch.

3 I had taken the job because I wanted to build things. My cousin had posted a video of a coffee table he built in a single weekend, and I imagined myself doing the same. Instead I spent my days rubbing the same board back and forth until my arms ached, while the saw sat in the corner like a dog I was forbidden to pet.

4 "When do I get to make something?" I finally asked him at the end of the third week.

5 Mr. Albescu ran his thumb along the board I had been sanding and frowned slightly, the way a doctor frowns at an X-ray. "You are making something," he said. "You are making your hands."

6 I thought this was the kind of thing old men said to avoid answering questions.

7 The following Monday he was called away to deliver a cabinet in Riverdale. "Sand the tabletop," he told me. "Nothing else." The door closed behind him, and the shop went quiet.

8 I lasted about twenty minutes. Then I took a scrap of oak from the pile and marked a line. I had watched him use the saw a hundred times. I knew where his hands went. I switched it on, and the blade woke up with a whine that filled the whole room.

9 The cut wandered. I felt it pull to the left, and when I switched the saw off, the edge of the board curved like a lazy river. Worse, the blade had left a dark burn mark where I had pushed too hard. I stood there with my heart pounding, listening for his truck.

10 I tried to hide it at the bottom of the scrap pile. But when Mr. Albescu came back, he looked once around the shop, the way he always did, and then he walked to the pile and pulled out my board as if it had called his name.

11 I waited for him to shout. Instead he turned the board over in his hands for a long time. Then he walked to a small pine cabinet that had stood in the corner all summer, pulled out its bottom drawer, and set the drawer on the workbench beside my board. The drawer was crooked. Its front sat at a slight angle, and one corner joint gapped open wide enough to slide a coin into.

12 "My first piece," he said. "I was fifteen. My teacher told me to wait, and I did not wait." He tapped the gap. "I keep it so I remember what hurry costs."

13 I looked at the crooked drawer, and then at the tools on the wall, each one returned to its outline, and for the first time I understood that the patience in this room had not always been there. It had been built, the way you build anything, one slow stroke at a time.

14 He handed me the sanding block. "The tabletop," he said. "Until it feels like the inside of your wrist."

15 This time I did not argue. I picked up the block and began, and I tried to feel the wood the way he did, listening with my fingers for the places that were not yet smooth.

passages.title: Learning to Float
passages.body:
In this poem, the speaker remembers a summer day when her father taught her to float in the ocean.

Learning to Float

     My father walked me out past the breakers
     at Rockaway, the August water slapping
     against my ribs, his hand flat under my back.
     "Lie back," he said. "The ocean wants to hold you."
 5   I did not believe him. I believed in fists,
     in kicking, in the hard work of not sinking.
     I thrashed like a fish dropped on a dock,
     swallowed salt, grabbed his arm with both hands,
     and every time I fought, the sea pulled down
10   as if my fear had weight and it could feel it.
     "You're fighting it," he said. "Stop fighting it."

     How do you stop fighting something
     bigger than all of Queens, something
     that has swallowed ships and never sleeps?
15   I lay back angry, certain I would sink.
     But then his hand slid out from under me,
     and I did not go under. I did not.
     The water rose up warm around my ears,
     and the beach went small and far away,
20   the gulls, the radios, the lifeguard's whistle,
     until there was only sky, enormous, blue,
     and the slow lift and settle of my breath.
     The sea had been holding me all along.
     It was only my struggle it could not carry.

25   Now, when the world comes at me in waves,
     a test, a slammed door, a night without sleep,
     I hear him: Lie back. Let it hold you.
     I spread my arms. I let the water rise.
     I trust what I could not see from the shore:
30   some things will carry us best
     when we stop trying to carry ourselves.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An unexpected result can be more valuable than a neat one because it can lead to better questions.
choices.explanation: Correct. Dr. Pruitt states the lesson directly in paragraph 12: "The surprises are where the science is. A result that disagrees with you is not a failure. It is information." Lena acts on that idea. She adds "NEW QUESTION: WAS IT THE HEAT?" to her poster (paragraph 13) and begins "sketching a third trial" on the way home (paragraph 14). The failed trial does not end her project. It points her toward a better question.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Friends who give advice usually do not understand the problems we face.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This choice takes a true detail and stretches it into a rule. Lena does think Danny made her problem "sound simple" (paragraph 4), but Danny appears only briefly. The passage is about what Lena learns from her failed trial, not about friends in general.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hard work and careful preparation are always rewarded with recognition.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This choice reverses the outcome. Lena prepares carefully, but paragraph 14 says "She did not win a ribbon that afternoon." Her reward is a new question, not recognition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Science fair judges care more about an honest speech than about accurate data.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This distorts what Dr. Pruitt values. She listens to the speech "without writing anything down" (paragraph 6) and becomes interested only when Lena shows the measurements in her notebook (paragraph 10). She cares about the data, not the speech.

questions.solutionExplanation: Dr. Pruitt states the lesson directly in paragraph 12: "The surprises are where the science is. A result that disagrees with you is not a failure. It is information." Lena acts on that idea. She adds "NEW QUESTION: WAS IT THE HEAT?" to her poster (paragraph 13) and begins "sketching a third trial" on the way home (paragraph 14). The failed trial does not end her project. It points her toward a better question.
questions.commonTrap: The choice about friends' advice is tempting because Danny's advice really is part of the conflict. But a theme has to cover the whole story. Danny appears in two paragraphs, while the change in how Lena sees her failed trial runs from paragraph 3 to the last line.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Which statement best describes how Lena changes over the course of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She goes from feeling confident about her project to feeling discouraged after the judges leave.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reverses her feelings. Paragraph 2 says the plants looked "green and confident" but "She did not feel either." After the judges leave, she is not discouraged. She revises her poster and plans a new trial (paragraphs 13 and 14).

choices.label: B
choices.text: She goes from trusting Danny's advice to believing that Danny was trying to ruin her project.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This is an overstatement. Lena chooses not to follow Danny's advice, but nothing suggests she thinks he meant her harm. Paragraph 4 shows only that he made the problem "sound simple."

choices.label: C
choices.text: She goes from hiding the results of her second trial to treating those results as the starting point for a new investigation.
choices.explanation: Correct. At the start, Lena hides the second trial. She slides the notebook "under the table, behind her backpack" (paragraph 3), and her poster shows only the first trial. By the end, she adds "TRIAL 2: SEE NOTEBOOK. NEW QUESTION: WAS IT THE HEAT?" to her poster (paragraph 13) and plans "a third trial, one with a thermometer beside every cup" (paragraph 14). The results she was ashamed of become the start of her next experiment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She goes from fearing public speaking to enjoying the attention of the judges.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Lena did practice her speech "in the bathroom mirror" (paragraph 6), but the passage never shows her enjoying attention. Her change is about how she sees her results, not about speaking in public.

questions.solutionExplanation: At the start, Lena hides the second trial. She slides the notebook "under the table, behind her backpack" (paragraph 3), and her poster shows only the first trial. By the end, she adds "TRIAL 2: SEE NOTEBOOK. NEW QUESTION: WAS IT THE HEAT?" to her poster (paragraph 13) and plans "a third trial, one with a thermometer beside every cup" (paragraph 14). The results she was ashamed of become the start of her next experiment.
questions.commonTrap: The confident-to-discouraged choice is tempting because Lena does not win a ribbon, so students assume she ends the story disappointed. The last paragraph shows the opposite: she is already sketching a third trial.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: How does paragraph 3 contribute to the development of the plot?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It explains the procedure Lena followed to create the bar graph on her poster.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Paragraph 3 mentions that Lena ran the experiment again, but it does not explain how she did it. Its purpose is to reveal the results she is hiding, not to describe her method.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reveals a secret that creates the central conflict Lena must face when the judge questions her.
choices.explanation: Correct. Paragraph 3 reveals what the poster "did not show": a second trial in which "the results had collapsed." Lena has hidden the notebook "behind her backpack." This secret is the conflict of the story. When Dr. Pruitt asks "How many times did you run it?" (paragraph 7), Lena must decide whether to reveal it, and her choice to say "Twice" (paragraph 9) is the turning point.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shows that Lena is careless about recording her measurements.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reverses the evidence. Paragraph 3 says "She had written every measurement" in her notebook, and paragraph 9 mentions her "careful handwriting." Lena hides her data, but she recorded it carefully.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It suggests that Lena will win a ribbon because her research is so thorough.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Nothing in paragraph 3 predicts a prize, and paragraph 14 says "She did not win a ribbon that afternoon."

questions.solutionExplanation: Paragraph 3 reveals what the poster "did not show": a second trial in which "the results had collapsed." Lena has hidden the notebook "behind her backpack." This secret is the conflict of the story. When Dr. Pruitt asks "How many times did you run it?" (paragraph 7), Lena must decide whether to reveal it, and her choice to say "Twice" (paragraph 9) is the turning point.
questions.commonTrap: Students who read paragraph 3 only for its facts may pick the choice about procedure, since the paragraph does discuss the experiment. A structure question asks what the paragraph does for the story. Here it sets up the secret that the rest of the plot turns on.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem:
Read this sentence from paragraph 3.

"She had written every measurement in her green composition notebook, and then she had closed the notebook and slid it under the table, behind her backpack, where it sat now like a secret holding its breath."

What does the phrase "like a secret holding its breath" suggest about the notebook?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is closed so tightly that no air can get inside it.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This is a literal reading of figurative language. A notebook cannot breathe. The phrase describes the tension of a hidden truth, not how tightly the notebook is closed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It makes Lena so nervous that she has trouble breathing during her speech.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This moves the description from the notebook to Lena. The phrase describes the notebook, and the passage never says Lena has trouble breathing while she speaks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It holds a secret that Lena has already forgotten about.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Lena has not forgotten. In paragraph 8 she "thought of the notebook behind her backpack," and it decides what she says to the judge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It seems to wait tensely, as if it might be revealed at any moment.
choices.explanation: Correct. The notebook is personified as "a secret holding its breath." A person holds their breath while waiting tensely for something to happen. The phrase suggests that the hidden notebook is waiting, as if it could be revealed at any moment. That is exactly what happens in paragraph 9, when Lena "pulled out the notebook."

questions.solutionExplanation: The notebook is personified as "a secret holding its breath." A person holds their breath while waiting tensely for something to happen. The phrase suggests that the hidden notebook is waiting, as if it could be revealed at any moment. That is exactly what happens in paragraph 9, when Lena "pulled out the notebook."
questions.commonTrap: The literal reading, that the notebook is shut tight, is tempting because "holding its breath" sounds like something sealed. On the SHSAT, a simile like this almost always describes a feeling or mood, here the tension of a truth waiting to come out.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Which two sentences from the passage best support the idea that Lena comes to see her failed trial in a new way? Select two answers.

choices.label: A
choices.text: "They looked green and confident." (paragraph 2)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This sentence describes the healthy plants on Lena's table, not her view of the failed trial. It comes before any change in her thinking.

choices.label: B
choices.text: "He had made it sound simple, the way people make everything sound simple when it is not their project." (paragraph 4)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This shows Lena's doubt about Danny's advice, but it does not show a new view of the failed trial. At this point she is still hiding the notebook.

choices.label: C
choices.text: "She heard herself say it, and something clicked, like a key finding its lock." (paragraph 11)
choices.explanation: Correct. As Lena explains that she moved the plants near the radiator, she suddenly understands that heat, not music, may explain her results. The failed trial now makes sense to her.

choices.label: D
choices.text: "Dr. Pruitt listened without writing anything down, which was worse than if she had written a great deal." (paragraph 6)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This shows Lena's nervousness during her speech. It says nothing about how she views the second trial.

choices.label: E
choices.text: "Then she took a marker from her backpack and, beneath the bar graph, in letters smaller than the title but just as blue, she wrote: TRIAL 2: SEE NOTEBOOK. NEW QUESTION: WAS IT THE HEAT?" (paragraph 13)
choices.explanation: Correct. Lena now puts the failed trial on her poster for everyone to see and turns it into a new question. This is the opposite of hiding it behind her backpack.

ms.solutionExplanation: The claim is that Lena comes to see the failed trial in a new way. In paragraph 11, while explaining the trials, she realizes the plants were moved near a radiator, and "something clicked, like a key finding its lock." The failed trial suddenly makes sense. In paragraph 13, she writes on her poster "TRIAL 2: SEE NOTEBOOK. NEW QUESTION: WAS IT THE HEAT?" The results she once hid are now displayed as the source of a new question.
