In paragraph 11, while explaining the trials, she realizes the plants were moved near a radiator, and "something clicked, like a key finding its lock." The failed trial suddenly makes sense. In paragraph 13, she writes on her poster "TRIAL 2: SEE NOTEBOOK. NEW QUESTION: WAS IT THE HEAT?" The results she once hid are now displayed as the source of a new question.
questions.commonTrap: The Danny sentence is tempting because it shows Lena questioning the plan to hide the trial. But doubting advice is not the same as seeing the trial differently. Only the "key finding its lock" moment and the new poster label show her new understanding.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem:
Read this sentence from paragraph 8.

"Then she thought of the notebook behind her backpack, and she found that she could not make her mouth say 'once.'"

What does this sentence suggest about Lena?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She has forgotten how many trials she ran because she is nervous.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This is too literal. Lena knows exactly how many trials she ran, and she answers "Twice" in paragraph 9. She cannot say "once" because it would be a lie, not because she forgot.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She is unwilling to hide the truth about her experiment, even though hiding it would be easier.
choices.explanation: Correct. Lena knows she ran the experiment twice. Saying "once" would be easy, because it would match her poster and follow Danny's advice. The words "she could not make her mouth say" suggest that something in her resists the lie. In the next paragraph she tells the truth. She answers "Twice" and admits, "The second time it didn't work." Her honesty wins out over the easier choice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She believes Dr. Pruitt has already seen the notebook under the table.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Nothing suggests Dr. Pruitt has seen the notebook. Lena has to pull it out and open it to the March pages in paragraph 9.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She wants to prove to Danny that his advice was foolish.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Danny is not at the table, and Lena's choice is about the truth of her project, not about proving anything to him.

questions.solutionExplanation: Lena knows she ran the experiment twice. Saying "once" would be easy, because it would match her poster and follow Danny's advice. The words "she could not make her mouth say" suggest that something in her resists the lie. In the next paragraph she tells the truth. She answers "Twice" and admits, "The second time it didn't work." Her honesty wins out over the easier choice.
questions.commonTrap: The "forgot" choice tempts students who read "could not make her mouth say" literally, as if she were unable to remember or speak. The phrase describes an inner struggle: she will not say something she knows is false.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Children should accept their parents' decisions without complaint.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Tomás does start helping at the end, but the story never says he was wrong to feel upset. He changes because of a shared memory with his father, not because he learns to stop complaining.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Moving is always harder for children than it is for adults.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reverses a key point. The father is also deeply affected: "His jaw was tight" (paragraph 10), and he admits, "If I stopped, I wasn't sure I'd start again" (paragraph 12).

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sharing memories of a place can help people face the loss of leaving it.
choices.explanation: Correct. Tomás begins the day refusing to help, angry about leaving "the only place I could remember" (paragraph 3). The turning point comes when he and his father trace the height marks, including the father's own childhood marks, onto paper. The shared memory lets both of them admit their sadness, and by the end Tomás "started taping boxes" (paragraph 14). The record of the place goes with them, and that helps them face leaving it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Old apartments should be preserved because of their history.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The story never argues for saving buildings. The landlord's painting is simply a fact that pushes Tomás to deal with the doorframe (paragraph 4).

questions.solutionExplanation: Tomás begins the day refusing to help, angry about leaving "the only place I could remember" (paragraph 3). The turning point comes when he and his father trace the height marks, including the father's own childhood marks, onto paper. The shared memory lets both of them admit their sadness, and by the end Tomás "started taping boxes" (paragraph 14). The record of the place goes with them, and that helps them face leaving it.
questions.commonTrap: The choice about obeying parents tempts students because Tomás's last action is to help pack. But the story is not about obedience. What changes him is understanding that his father shares his loss.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: The narrator's feelings change as the passage moves forward. Match each paragraph with the feeling the narrator shows most strongly in that paragraph.

dnd.instruction: Move the correct feeling into each box. Not all feelings will be used.

pool.explanation: Belongs with paragraph 2. Tomás has "decided not to help" and calls this "the only protest I had left." He sits on the radiator and watches everyone else work.
Belongs with paragraph 6. "You cannot pack a doorframe." He feels "something hot rise in my throat" because a stranger will "erase eleven years in a few strokes," and he can do nothing to stop it.
Belongs with paragraph 14. Tomás carries the roll himself, "holding it upright in both hands," doing the job his father gave him, and then he goes back up to help pack.
Not used. Nothing in these paragraphs is presented as funny. The playful phrase "the beanstalk year" belongs to his mother in paragraph 7, and even there Tomás is not amused.
Not used. Tomás does start helping in paragraph 14, but the passage never says he feels ashamed. He helps because he understands his father, not because he is embarrassed.

dnd.solutionExplanation: Paragraph 2: Tomás has "decided not to help" and calls it "the only protest I had left," which shows stubborn resentment. Paragraph 6: "You cannot pack a doorframe," and he feels "something hot rise in my throat" knowing a stranger will "erase eleven years in a few strokes," which shows helpless grief. Paragraph 14: he carries the roll down the stairs "holding it upright in both hands the way you would carry a lit candle," then starts taping boxes, which shows careful responsibility.

questions.solutionExplanation: Paragraph 2: Tomás has "decided not to help" and calls it "the only protest I had left," which shows stubborn resentment. Paragraph 6: "You cannot pack a doorframe," and he feels "something hot rise in my throat" knowing a stranger will "erase eleven years in a few strokes," which shows helpless grief. Paragraph 14: he carries the roll down the stairs "holding it upright in both hands the way you would carry a lit candle," then starts taping boxes, which shows careful responsibility.
questions.commonTrap: Students often place "embarrassed guilt" in paragraph 14 because Tomás finally starts helping, so they assume he feels bad about refusing earlier. The text shows care, not shame: he holds the roll "upright in both hands" like something precious.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: How do paragraphs 8 and 9 contribute to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They reveal that the doorframe also holds the father's childhood, which leads Tomás to see his father's behavior differently.
choices.explanation: Correct. In paragraphs 8 and 9, Tomás finds older marks labeled "R.M." and learns they are his father's: "This was her apartment before it was ours. I grew up in that kitchen." This discovery leads Tomás to see his father differently. Right after it, he notices "His jaw was tight" and that his father "wasn't whistling" (paragraph 10), and the two finally talk about how they feel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They introduce Tomás's grandmother as the character whose feelings matter most in the story.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The grandmother appears only through her handwriting and the fact that the apartment was hers. The story's focus stays on Tomás and his father.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They explain why the landlord has decided to paint the apartment.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The landlord's painting is mentioned in paragraph 4 and is never explained. Paragraphs 8 and 9 are about the family's history in the apartment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They prove that Tomás was wrong to want to stay in Brooklyn.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This overstates the effect. The discovery deepens the sense of loss, since the family has lived there for two generations. It does not show that Tomás's feelings were wrong.

questions.solutionExplanation: In paragraphs 8 and 9, Tomás finds older marks labeled "R.M." and learns they are his father's: "This was her apartment before it was ours. I grew up in that kitchen." This discovery leads Tomás to see his father differently. Right after it, he notices "His jaw was tight" and that his father "wasn't whistling" (paragraph 10), and the two finally talk about how they feel.
questions.commonTrap: The grandmother choice is tempting because her handwriting is the surprising new detail. But the marks matter because they belong to the father, and they change how Tomás understands him.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem:
Read this sentence from paragraph 13.

"We traced his marks too, onto the same strip of paper, his faint lines below my dark ones, like the roots of a plant beneath its stem."

What does the comparison to "the roots of a plant" suggest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The packing paper will be used to wrap the family's houseplants.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This is a literal reading. No real plants are mentioned. The comparison describes how the marks relate to each other, not what the paper will be used for.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The father's past is the foundation that Tomás's own growth comes from.
choices.explanation: Correct. Roots grow underground, below the stem, and they feed and hold up the plant. Placing the father's "faint lines below my dark ones" like roots suggests that the father's childhood in the apartment is the foundation that Tomás's own growth comes from. The image connects the two generations on one strip of paper.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The father's marks are more important than Tomás's marks.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Roots and stem are parts of the same plant. The image connects the two sets of marks. It does not rank one above the other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tomás has nearly stopped growing taller.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Nothing in the comparison or the passage suggests that Tomás's growth is ending. The image is about where his growth comes from.

questions.solutionExplanation: Roots grow underground, below the stem, and they feed and hold up the plant. Placing the father's "faint lines below my dark ones" like roots suggests that the father's childhood in the apartment is the foundation that Tomás's own growth comes from. The image connects the two generations on one strip of paper.
questions.commonTrap: Students who see the father's marks placed "below" may think the image ranks them as more or less important. Roots are not lesser than a stem. They are what the stem grows from, which is the connection the image draws.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Which sentence from the passage best shows that the move affects Tomás's father more than he first lets on?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "He wrapped plates in newspaper, taped boxes shut with one long screech of tape, and whistled under his breath." (paragraph 3)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This shows the father's calm surface, the behavior that makes Tomás think his father does not care. It does not show the hidden feelings underneath.

choices.label: B
choices.text: "My parents listened, nodded, and signed the lease anyway." (paragraph 2)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This shows the parents' decision to move, not how the father feels about leaving.

choices.label: C
choices.text: "I had always known that, in the way you know facts about your parents without ever really thinking about them." (paragraph 10)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This sentence is about Tomás's own awareness of where his father grew up. It does not show the father's emotion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: "His jaw was tight. For the first time all morning, he wasn't whistling." (paragraph 10)
choices.explanation: Correct. All morning, Tomás reads his father's whistling and fast packing as a sign that "He didn't seem to care at all" (paragraph 3). In paragraph 10, once the father's marks are found, Tomás notices "His jaw was tight. For the first time all morning, he wasn't whistling." The tight jaw and the missing whistle show feelings the father had been hiding.

questions.solutionExplanation: All morning, Tomás reads his father's whistling and fast packing as a sign that "He didn't seem to care at all" (paragraph 3). In paragraph 10, once the father's marks are found, Tomás notices "His jaw was tight. For the first time all morning, he wasn't whistling." The tight jaw and the missing whistle show feelings the father had been hiding.
questions.commonTrap: The whistling sentence from paragraph 3 is tempting because it describes the father directly. But it shows what he lets on, not what he feels. The question asks for the moment the hidden feeling shows through.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: In paragraph 12, the father says, "If I stopped, I wasn't sure I'd start again." What does this statement suggest about him?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He kept busy so that his sadness about leaving would not overwhelm him.
choices.explanation: Correct. The father kept packing "quickly and without comment" (paragraph 3) and whistled all morning. When he explains, "Somebody had to keep taping boxes," and adds, "If I stopped, I wasn't sure I'd start again," he admits that staying busy kept his sadness under control. His "slow shrug, heavier than usual" (paragraph 12) shows the weight he had been carrying.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He was rushing because the moving truck was about to arrive.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reads the line as a practical schedule problem. No truck or deadline is mentioned, and the father's "slow shrug, heavier than usual" points to emotion, not time pressure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He did not want to move and was planning to stay behind in Brooklyn.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This overstates his feelings. He is sad about leaving, but he keeps packing and gives Tomás a job for the move. Nothing suggests he plans to stay.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He blamed Tomás's mother for the family's decision to move.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The passage never shows any blame. Both parents "listened, nodded, and signed the lease" (paragraph 2).

questions.solutionExplanation: The father kept packing "quickly and without comment" (paragraph 3) and whistled all morning. When he explains, "Somebody had to keep taping boxes," and adds, "If I stopped, I wasn't sure I'd start again," he admits that staying busy kept his sadness under control. His "slow shrug, heavier than usual" (paragraph 12) shows the weight he had been carrying.
questions.commonTrap: The moving-truck choice is tempting because "stopped" and "start again" sound like they describe work. In context, the father is answering Tomás's charge that he "acted like it was nothing," so the line is about his feelings.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Which statement best describes the central idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A girl wins back her place at first board by studying her rival's games and finding the weaknesses that others missed.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Nadia does list Owen's weaknesses, but she never wins back first board. In paragraph 15 the question of who sits there is "still there," just smaller.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A talented young player proves to his older teammates that speed matters more than skill in chess.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This distorts Owen's role. His games show boldness, not speed winning over skill, and Nadia still finds real mistakes in them (paragraph 7).

choices.label: C
choices.text: A coach teaches his players that their positions in the team lineup do not really matter.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Coach Bekele never says this, and Nadia's ranking "still mattered" at the end (paragraph 15).

choices.label: D
choices.text: While studying a rival's games, a girl realizes her own caution may have held her back, and she chooses to learn from him instead of resenting him.
choices.explanation: Correct. Nadia loses first board to Owen and resents it ("It's not just a list," paragraph 5). Assigned to study his games, she sees that he plays without fear, and she begins to suspect her "discipline" "had another name" (paragraph 9). She writes "WHAT I SHOULD STEAL" (paragraph 10) and asks Owen to teach her (paragraph 14). The passage is mainly about this shift from resentment to learning.

questions.solutionExplanation: Nadia loses first board to Owen and resents it ("It's not just a list," paragraph 5). Assigned to study his games, she sees that he plays without fear, and she begins to suspect her "discipline" "had another name" (paragraph 9). She writes "WHAT I SHOULD STEAL" (paragraph 10) and asks Owen to teach her (paragraph 14). The passage is mainly about this shift from resentment to learning.
questions.commonTrap: The "wins back first board" choice tempts students who expect a rivalry story to end in victory. This passage turns away from that ending. The lineup never changes. Nadia's thinking does.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Which two statements best describe how Nadia changes over the course of the passage? Select two answers.

choices.label: A
choices.text: She decides that her place in the lineup no longer matters to her at all.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This is an overstatement. Paragraph 15 says the question of first board "was still there. It still mattered." It has only become smaller.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She moves from resenting Owen's promotion to treating him as someone she can learn from.
choices.explanation: Correct. She is hurt by the new lineup in paragraphs 3 through 5, but in paragraph 14 she asks Owen to explain his thinking about "Move nine. The queen."

choices.label: C
choices.text: She becomes convinced that Owen's frequent mistakes make him a weak player.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reverses her conclusion. She does circle his mistakes at first, but paragraph 8 says "there were many more wins," and she ends up wanting to learn from him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She begins to question whether the careful style she called discipline was really a form of fear.
choices.explanation: Correct. In paragraph 9 she "had always called it discipline," but next to Owen's "fearless" games she "began to suspect it had another name." Her accepted draws "because a draw could not hurt her ranking" point to fear of losing.

choices.label: E
choices.text: She loses trust in Coach Bekele's judgment and stops listening to his advice.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Nothing supports this. Nadia completes his assignment and brings him her notes, and he praises her work (paragraph 11).

ms.solutionExplanation: Nadia starts out resenting Owen's promotion: the lineup feels like losing "the place where she lived" (paragraph 5). By the end, she asks Owen to show her his thinking (paragraph 14), treating him as someone to learn from. She also questions her own style. She "had always called it discipline," but after seeing Owen's "fearless" games, she "began to suspect it had another name" (paragraph 9), suggesting her caution was really fear of losing.

questions.solutionExplanation: Nadia starts out resenting Owen's promotion: the lineup feels like losing "the place where she lived" (paragraph 5). By the end, she asks Owen to show her his thinking (paragraph 14), treating him as someone to learn from. She also questions her own style. She "had always called it discipline," but after seeing Owen's "fearless" games, she "began to suspect it had another name" (paragraph 9), suggesting her caution was really fear of losing.
questions.commonTrap: The "no longer matters at all" choice is the most tempting wrong answer because the last paragraph says first board seemed "a much smaller question." Smaller is not gone: the same paragraph says "It still mattered."

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: How does paragraph 6 contribute to the development of the plot?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that Coach Bekele regrets moving Nadia to second board.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Coach Bekele calls Nadia "my best analyst," but nothing suggests he regrets the new lineup. He asks her to help the team prepare for the finals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reveals that Nadia secretly plans to make Owen lose at the city finals.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The coach wants the team to know Owen's weaknesses because "Other schools will be studying him." Nadia never plans to hurt Owen's chances.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It gives Nadia a task that forces her to study Owen's games closely, which leads to her change in thinking.
choices.explanation: Correct. In paragraph 6, Coach Bekele asks Nadia to "Figure out his weaknesses" and hands her a folder of Owen's games. Nadia sees this as making things worse ("It got worse"), but the assignment forces her to study Owen's games closely. That close study is what leads to her realization in paragraphs 8 and 9 and her change at the end.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It explains why Owen plays faster than the other members of the team.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Paragraph 6 does not explain Owen's speed. It sets up Nadia's assignment.

questions.solutionExplanation: In paragraph 6, Coach Bekele asks Nadia to "Figure out his weaknesses" and hands her a folder of Owen's games. Nadia sees this as making things worse ("It got worse"), but the assignment forces her to study Owen's games closely. That close study is what leads to her realization in paragraphs 8 and 9 and her change at the end.
questions.commonTrap: Students who take "It got worse" at face value may think paragraph 6 just adds another insult. Its real job in the plot is to put Owen's games in front of Nadia, which makes her change possible.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem:
Read this sentence from paragraph 5.

"She did not explain, because she did not know how to say that first board had become a kind of address, the place where she lived."

What does this description suggest about first board?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It had become an important part of how Nadia saw herself.
choices.explanation: Correct. An address is where a person lives. Calling first board "a kind of address, the place where she lived" suggests that the position had become part of who Nadia is, not just a spot on a list. That is why she insists "It's not just a list" (paragraph 5).

choices.label: B
choices.text: It was located so close to her home that she could walk there.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reads "address" literally. First board is a position on the team, not a physical place near her home.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It was where she spent so much time that school felt like her home.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This is another literal reading. The sentence is about what the position means to her, not how many hours she spends at school.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It was a position she was ready to give up to a younger player.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reverses her attitude. She insists "It's not just a list" because the position means so much to her.

questions.solutionExplanation: An address is where a person lives. Calling first board "a kind of address, the place where she lived" suggests that the position had become part of who Nadia is, not just a spot on a list. That is why she insists "It's not just a list" (paragraph 5).
questions.commonTrap: Two choices read "address" and "the place where she lived" as real places. The phrase is a metaphor. Strong readers ask what the comparison says about Nadia's feelings.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Which detail from the passage best supports the idea that Nadia's style of play had been too cautious?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "Before every match she lined up her pieces so that each knight faced exactly forward" (paragraph 1)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This shows that Nadia is neat and orderly before a game, but it says nothing about how cautiously she plays once the game begins.

choices.label: B
choices.text: "the draws she had accepted when she was ahead because a draw could not hurt her ranking" (paragraph 9)
choices.explanation: Correct. Paragraph 9 lists "the draws she had accepted when she was ahead because a draw could not hurt her ranking." Accepting a tie while winning, only to protect a ranking, is overly cautious play. It is the clearest sign that her "discipline" may really be fear of losing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: "She circled each one in red with grim satisfaction." (paragraph 7)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This shows Nadia's pleasure in finding Owen's mistakes, not her own style of play.

choices.label: D
choices.text: "In his third week he beat Nadia, in a game so fast and so strange" (paragraph 2)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes Owen's style and his win. It does not show that Nadia's play was cautious.

questions.solutionExplanation: Paragraph 9 lists "the draws she had accepted when she was ahead because a draw could not hurt her ranking." Accepting a tie while winning, only to protect a ranking, is overly cautious play. It is the clearest sign that her "discipline" may really be fear of losing.
questions.commonTrap: The knights-lined-up detail is tempting because it shows a careful personality, and students link careful with cautious. But the question is about her play during games. Only the accepted draws show caution at the board.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: In paragraph 10, Nadia titles the second page of her notes "WHAT I SHOULD STEAL." This title mainly suggests that Nadia

choices.label: A
choices.text: plans to take Owen's score sheets and claim his wins as her own.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reads "steal" literally. Nadia returns the folder to Coach Bekele, and nothing suggests she wants credit for Owen's games.

choices.label: B
choices.text: wants Coach Bekele to believe that Owen has been cheating.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Nothing in the passage suggests cheating. The coach calls the page "the most useful thing anyone's given me all year," which would not fit an accusation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: is willing to borrow ideas from Owen's bold style to improve her own game.
choices.explanation: Correct. Nadia's first page lists Owen's weaknesses, but her second page is titled "WHAT I SHOULD STEAL." Here "steal" means borrow ideas. After seeing that Owen attacks fearlessly and wins far more than he loses, Nadia is willing to adopt parts of his bold style. In paragraph 14 she asks him to explain his thinking.

choices.label: D
choices.text: has given up on finding any weaknesses in Owen's play.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Her first page "listed Owen's weaknesses, as she had been asked." She found weaknesses and also found things worth learning.

questions.solutionExplanation: Nadia's first page lists Owen's weaknesses, but her second page is titled "WHAT I SHOULD STEAL." Here "steal" means borrow ideas. After seeing that Owen attacks fearlessly and wins far more than he loses, Nadia is willing to adopt parts of his bold style. In paragraph 14 she asks him to explain his thinking.
questions.commonTrap: The literal reading of "steal" is the trap. Students should ask what Nadia wants to take from Owen: his fearless way of playing, not his property.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stories that change over time are lies and cannot be trusted.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This is the narrator's fear in paragraph 7, not the lesson of the story. By the end she sees the changing story as meaningful, not false.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A family story can hold an important truth even when its details change.
choices.explanation: Correct. The two versions of Lola's story have different weather, money, and strangers, yet Lola says the important part never changes: "someone on that boat was kind to me, and that I decided, right there in the middle of the water, that I would stay" (paragraph 12). The narrator ends by describing a story that "bends to fit whoever is listening" without "ever stopping being a river" (paragraph 14). The story's truth survives its changing details.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Arriving in a new country can be a frightening experience.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Lola does say she was "nineteen and frightened" (paragraph 12), but this is a true detail, not the message of the whole passage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Older people remember the past more clearly than young people expect.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reverses what Lola says: "I don't remember the weather" (paragraph 12).

questions.solutionExplanation: The two versions of Lola's story have different weather, money, and strangers, yet Lola says the important part never changes: "someone on that boat was kind to me, and that I decided, right there in the middle of the water, that I would stay" (paragraph 12). The narrator ends by describing a story that "bends to fit whoever is listening" without "ever stopping being a river" (paragraph 14). The story's truth survives its changing details.
questions.commonTrap: The "frightening experience" choice is tempting because it is true in the story. A theme has to explain why the story was told. This one is about what makes a story true, not about immigration in general.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Which statement best describes how the narrator's view of the ferry story changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She first admires the story, but she comes to suspect that her grandmother invented the entire trip.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reverses the ending. Lola confirms that the trip happened and that "someone on that boat was kind to me" (paragraph 12). The narrator ends up valuing the story more, not doubting it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She first finds the story boring, but she comes to resent her grandmother for changing it.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The first half is close, since she listens with "half my attention" (paragraph 4). But her resentment in paragraph 8 fades. She ends up thinking about her grandmother's kindness, not her own anger.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She first doubts the story, but she comes to believe that every detail of the Thanksgiving version is accurate.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. She never decides that one version is the accurate one. She types up "both versions" side by side (paragraph 14), and Lola says the answer is "Both" and "Neither" (paragraph 12).

choices.label: D
choices.text: She first treats it as a familiar set of facts that will make her project easy, but she comes to see it as a gift her grandmother shapes for each listener.
choices.explanation: Correct. At first the narrator chooses Lola's story "because it seemed easy" and listens "with half my attention" (paragraphs 3 and 4). She treats it as a set of facts to record. After Lola explains that she shapes the story for each listener, the narrator understands that Lola chose a "bright morning" because her granddaughter was nervous (paragraph 10). By the end, the narrator values the story as a gift: her grandmother "had known I was nervous before I told anyone" (paragraph 14).

questions.solutionExplanation: At first the narrator chooses Lola's story "because it seemed easy" and listens "with half my attention" (paragraphs 3 and 4). She treats it as a set of facts to record. After Lola explains that she shapes the story for each listener, the narrator understands that Lola chose a "bright morning" because her granddaughter was nervous (paragraph 10). By the end, the narrator values the story as a gift: her grandmother "had known I was nervous before I told anyone" (paragraph 14).
questions.commonTrap: The "boring, then resentful" choice is tempting because each half matches a moment in the passage. But it stops too early. The narrator's accusation in paragraph 8 is a middle step, not where she ends up.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Put the events from the passage in the order in which they happen.

dnd.instruction: Move one event into each box. Not all events will be used.

pool.text: The narrator records Lola telling the story at the kitchen table.
pool.explanation: First. In paragraph 4 the narrator sets her phone on the table and Lola tells the story.

pool.text: The narrator notices new details while typing up the recording.
pool.explanation: Second. In paragraph 5, "That night, typing up the recording, I noticed the problem."

pool.text: The narrator listens to the version in her uncle's Thanksgiving video.
pool.explanation: Third. In paragraph 6, after playing her recording back, she finds the video from two years ago.

pool.text: Lola explains that she shapes the story for whoever is listening.
pool.explanation: Fourth. This happens "The next afternoon" (paragraph 8), when Lola explains her choices in paragraph 10.

pool.text: The narrator presents both versions to her class and answers questions.
pool.explanation: Not used. In paragraph 7 the narrator only imagines a classmate asking which version is real. The passage never shows her presenting to the class.

pool.text: Lola refuses to let the narrator record the story.
pool.explanation: Not used. Lola agrees to be recorded. In paragraph 4 she "folded her hands and told the story."

dnd.solutionExplanation: The narrator records Lola at the kitchen table (paragraph 4). That night, typing up the recording, she notices new details (paragraph 5). Then she finds her uncle's video of the older version (paragraph 6). The next afternoon, Lola explains that she shapes the story for whoever is listening (paragraph 10).

questions.solutionExplanation: The narrator records Lola at the kitchen table (paragraph 4). That night, typing up the recording, she notices new details (paragraph 5). Then she finds her uncle's video of the older version (paragraph 6). The next afternoon, Lola explains that she shapes the story for whoever is listening (paragraph 10).
questions.commonTrap: Students sometimes place the classroom presentation in the sequence because paragraph 7 describes it vividly. The narrator only imagines it. An event that a character pictures has not happened in the plot.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem:
Read this sentence from paragraph 14.

"Underneath, where my paragraphs about the 1970s were supposed to go, I wrote about a story that bends to fit whoever is listening, the way a river bends to fit its banks without ever stopping being a river."

What does the comparison to a river suggest about Lola's story?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It changes its details to suit each listener while keeping the same essential meaning.
choices.explanation: Correct. A river changes its shape to follow its banks, but it is still the same river. The narrator compares Lola's story to this: it "bends to fit whoever is listening" by changing details like the weather and the stranger, but its core, that someone was kind and Lola chose to stay, does not change.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It becomes weaker and less clear each time Lola tells it.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The river image stresses that the story never stops "being a river." Nothing suggests the story fades or weakens.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is mostly about the water Lola crossed on the ferry.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This is a literal reading. The ferry crossed water, but the river comparison describes how the story changes, not what it is about.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is impossible to control, like a river that floods its banks.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The sentence describes a river that "bends to fit its banks," not one that floods them. Lola shapes each telling on purpose.

questions.solutionExplanation: A river changes its shape to follow its banks, but it is still the same river. The narrator compares Lola's story to this: it "bends to fit whoever is listening" by changing details like the weather and the stranger, but its core, that someone was kind and Lola chose to stay, does not change.
questions.commonTrap: The flooding choice tempts students who picture a river as wild and powerful. The sentence describes a river fitting itself to its banks. That calm, purposeful bending matches how Lola chooses details for each listener.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the idea that Lola changes her story to fit what her listener needs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "I was nineteen and frightened, and I don't remember the weather." (paragraph 12)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This explains why the details can vary, since Lola does not remember them. It does not show that she chooses details based on her listener.

choices.label: B
choices.text: "She did not look surprised." (paragraph 9)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This shows that Lola expected the question, but it does not explain how or why she changes the story.

choices.label: C
choices.text: "You are nervous, though you don't say so. So I gave you a bright morning and a woman who said welcome." (paragraph 10)
choices.explanation: Correct. In paragraph 10 Lola explains why the narrator heard a different version: "You are nervous, though you don't say so. So I gave you a bright morning and a woman who said welcome." The word "So" connects the listener's need (nervousness) to Lola's choice of details. This directly shows her fitting the story to the listener.

choices.label: D
choices.text: "Every Thanksgiving, after the pie and before the dishes, my grandmother told the ferry story." (paragraph 1)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This shows that the story is a family tradition, not that Lola adjusts it for different listeners.

questions.solutionExplanation: In paragraph 10 Lola explains why the narrator heard a different version: "You are nervous, though you don't say so. So I gave you a bright morning and a woman who said welcome." The word "So" connects the listener's need (nervousness) to Lola's choice of details. This directly shows her fitting the story to the listener.
questions.commonTrap: The "I don't remember the weather" quotation is the strongest trap. It is close in topic, since it explains why the details change. But the claim is about fitting the listener's needs, and only the paragraph 10 quotation connects a listener to a chosen detail.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: In paragraph 7, the narrator's stomach sinks mainly because she

choices.label: A
choices.text: suspects that her grandmother is becoming ill and forgetting things.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Nothing in paragraph 7 mentions illness. The narrator's worry is about her project, as the next sentence explains.

choices.label: B
choices.text: realizes that she accidentally deleted part of the recording.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The recording is complete. She "played it back three times" in paragraph 6.

choices.label: C
choices.text: is upset that her uncle recorded the story without asking permission.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The narrator uses her uncle's video to compare versions. She never objects to it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: worries that her project will fall apart if she cannot say which version of the story is true.
choices.explanation: Correct. Paragraph 7 gives the reason directly after "My stomach sank": "My whole project depended on the story being true, and now I had two stories, and they could not both be." She then imagines a classmate asking which version was real and having "nothing to say." She is worried that her project will fall apart.

questions.solutionExplanation: Paragraph 7 gives the reason directly after "My stomach sank": "My whole project depended on the story being true, and now I had two stories, and they could not both be." She then imagines a classmate asking which version was real and having "nothing to say." She is worried that her project will fall apart.
questions.commonTrap: The illness choice tempts students who bring in outside assumptions about grandparents and memory. The passage states the narrator's reason in the very next sentence: her project "depended on the story being true."

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Young people should never be allowed to use dangerous tools.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This stretches a detail into a rule. The narrator is not allowed to touch the saw yet, but the story is about learning patience, not a permanent ban on tools.

choices.label: B
choices.text: True experts are people who have never made serious mistakes.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reverses the story's point. Mr. Albescu, the expert, keeps his own crooked drawer to remember a serious mistake (paragraph 12).

choices.label: C
choices.text: Online videos make difficult tasks look easier than they are.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The cousin's video appears only in paragraph 3 as part of the narrator's expectations. It is a minor detail, not the message of the passage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Real skill is built slowly, and mistakes can teach the value of patience.
choices.explanation: Correct. The narrator wants to skip ahead to building, rushes a cut on the saw, and ruins the board. Mr. Albescu responds by showing the crooked drawer he made as a hurried fifteen-year-old: "I keep it so I remember what hurry costs" (paragraph 12). The narrator then understands that patience "had been built, the way you build anything, one slow stroke at a time" (paragraph 13). Skill grows slowly, and a mistake can teach that lesson.

questions.solutionExplanation: The narrator wants to skip ahead to building, rushes a cut on the saw, and ruins the board. Mr. Albescu responds by showing the crooked drawer he made as a hurried fifteen-year-old: "I keep it so I remember what hurry costs" (paragraph 12). The narrator then understands that patience "had been built, the way you build anything, one slow stroke at a time" (paragraph 13). Skill grows slowly, and a mistake can teach that lesson.
questions.commonTrap: The online-video choice tempts students because it is reasonable and appears in the passage. But the video is mentioned once and never returns. A theme has to be developed across the whole story.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: How does the narrator's attitude toward sanding change over the course of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The narrator first enjoys sanding but later finds it boring compared with using the saw.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reverses the order. The narrator is frustrated with sanding from the start (paragraph 3) and accepts it at the end (paragraph 15).

choices.label: B
choices.text: The narrator first sees sanding as a pointless delay but later treats it as a way to develop the careful touch the craft requires.
choices.explanation: Correct. Early on, sanding is something the narrator puts up with while wanting the saw. Days spent "rubbing the same board back and forth until my arms ached" (paragraph 3) lead to the question "When do I get to make something?" (paragraph 4). After the ruined board and the crooked drawer, the narrator sands without arguing and tries "to feel the wood the way he did, listening with my fingers" (paragraph 15). Sanding has become training for the hands, as Mr. Albescu said: "You are making your hands."

choices.label: C
choices.text: The narrator first considers sanding too difficult but later realizes it is the easiest task in the shop.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The narrator's complaint is that sanding is slow and dull, not difficult. At the end, sanding is treated as serious work, not as easy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The narrator first sands to please Mr. Albescu but later sands out of fear of losing the job.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Nothing suggests the narrator fears being fired. Mr. Albescu responds calmly, and the narrator's new effort comes from understanding, not fear.

questions.solutionExplanation: Early on, sanding is something the narrator puts up with while wanting the saw. Days spent "rubbing the same board back and forth until my arms ached" (paragraph 3) lead to the question "When do I get to make something?" (paragraph 4). After the ruined board and the crooked drawer, the narrator sands without arguing and tries "to feel the wood the way he did, listening with my fingers" (paragraph 15). Sanding has become training for the hands, as Mr. Albescu said: "You are making your hands."
questions.commonTrap: The fear-of-being-fired choice is tempting because the narrator is clearly scared after the ruined cut ("my heart pounding"). But that fear comes before Mr. Albescu returns. The change at the end comes from what the drawer teaches.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: How do paragraphs 11 and 12 contribute to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They show that Mr. Albescu once made the same kind of mistake, which turns the moment from a punishment into a lesson.
choices.explanation: Correct. The narrator expects Mr. Albescu to shout (paragraph 11). Instead, he brings out his own crooked first drawer and explains, "My teacher told me to wait, and I did not wait" (paragraph 12). Revealing that he once made the same kind of mistake turns a moment of possible punishment into a lesson. That lesson leads straight to the narrator's realization in paragraph 13.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They explain how to repair a drawer whose corner joint has come apart.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The gap in the drawer is described, but no repair is explained. Mr. Albescu keeps the drawer unrepaired on purpose, as a reminder.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They show that Mr. Albescu is furious about the damage to his saw.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reverses his reaction. Paragraph 11 begins "I waited for him to shout. Instead," and the saw was never damaged.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They reveal that the pine cabinet was built by Mr. Albescu's teacher.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Mr. Albescu calls the drawer "My first piece" (paragraph 12). His teacher is mentioned only as the person who told him to wait.

questions.solutionExplanation: The narrator expects Mr. Albescu to shout (paragraph 11). Instead, he brings out his own crooked first drawer and explains, "My teacher told me to wait, and I did not wait" (paragraph 12). Revealing that he once made the same kind of mistake turns a moment of possible punishment into a lesson. That lesson leads straight to the narrator's realization in paragraph 13.
questions.commonTrap: Students who skim may think the drawer belongs to Mr. Albescu's teacher, since the teacher is mentioned in the same line. Read the exact words: "My first piece." The drawer is his own mistake, which is why it teaches the narrator so much.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem:
Read this sentence from paragraph 3.

"Instead I spent my days rubbing the same board back and forth until my arms ached, while the saw sat in the corner like a dog I was forbidden to pet."

What does the comparison suggest about the saw?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It was old and noisy, like a dog that barks all day.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Nothing in the comparison refers to noise or age. The phrase "forbidden to pet" points to wanting something you cannot touch.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It was dangerous and likely to attack anyone who came near it.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This misreads the image. People want to pet friendly dogs, not dangerous ones. The comparison is about temptation, not threat.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It tempted the narrator even though the narrator was not allowed to use it.
choices.explanation: Correct. A dog you are forbidden to pet is close by and appealing, but off-limits. The simile shows that the saw tempted the narrator the whole time it sat in the corner, even though it was "not allowed" (paragraph 2). That temptation pays off in paragraph 8, when the narrator uses the saw anyway.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It belonged to someone other than Mr. Albescu.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Nothing suggests the saw belongs to anyone else. The narrator watched Mr. Albescu "use the saw a hundred times" (paragraph 8).

questions.solutionExplanation: A dog you are forbidden to pet is close by and appealing, but off-limits. The simile shows that the saw tempted the narrator the whole time it sat in the corner, even though it was "not allowed" (paragraph 2). That temptation pays off in paragraph 8, when the narrator uses the saw anyway.
questions.commonTrap: The "dangerous" choice is tempting because table saws really are dangerous. But the simile is about wanting to pet the dog. Ask what feeling the comparison gives the narrator: desire for something off-limits.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Which two sentences best support the idea that the narrator's attitude toward the work has changed by the end of the passage? Select two answers.

choices.label: A
choices.text: "This time I did not argue." (paragraph 15)
choices.explanation: Correct. The words "This time" point back to the earlier complaint in paragraph 4. The narrator now accepts the sanding task.

choices.label: B
choices.text: "I thought this was the kind of thing old men said to avoid answering questions." (paragraph 6)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This shows the narrator's earlier attitude, dismissing Mr. Albescu's advice. It is the attitude the narrator later moves away from.

choices.label: C
choices.text: "I had watched him use the saw a hundred times." (paragraph 8)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This shows the overconfidence that leads to the ruined cut. It comes before the change.

choices.label: D
choices.text: "I picked up the block and began, and I tried to feel the wood the way he did, listening with my fingers for the places that were not yet smooth." (paragraph 15)
choices.explanation: Correct. The narrator now pays close attention to the wood, the way Mr. Albescu does. This is the careful touch he meant by "You are making your hands."

choices.label: E
choices.text: "I switched it on, and the blade woke up with a whine that filled the whole room." (paragraph 8)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes the saw starting during the narrator's impatient attempt. It shows no change in attitude.

ms.solutionExplanation: The claim is about the narrator's attitude at the end. In paragraph 15, "This time I did not argue" contrasts with the earlier complaint, "When do I get to make something?" (paragraph 4). The narrator also tries "to feel the wood the way he did, listening with my fingers for the places that were not yet smooth," which shows real attention to the work instead of impatience.

questions.solutionExplanation: The claim is about the narrator's attitude at the end. In paragraph 15, "This time I did not argue" contrasts with the earlier complaint, "When do I get to make something?" (paragraph 4). The narrator also tries "to feel the wood the way he did, listening with my fingers for the places that were not yet smooth," which shows real attention to the work instead of impatience.
questions.commonTrap: The paragraph 6 sentence is tempting because it clearly states an attitude. But it is the before picture. The question asks for evidence of the change by the end, so the answers must come from after the turning point.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Based on paragraphs 10 through 14, why does Mr. Albescu most likely respond calmly to the ruined board?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He believes the board can easily be repaired, so no real harm was done.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Nothing suggests he plans to fix the board. He studies it and then compares it to his own crooked drawer, which he never repaired.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He recognizes his own youthful impatience in the narrator's mistake and wants to teach rather than punish.
choices.explanation: Correct. Mr. Albescu "turned the board over in his hands for a long time" (paragraph 11) and then brings out his own first piece, made when "My teacher told me to wait, and I did not wait" (paragraph 12). He sees his younger self in the narrator's mistake. Instead of shouting, he uses the moment to teach, and he hands back the sanding block (paragraph 14), showing he still wants the narrator to learn.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He has decided the narrator is not suited to woodworking and sees no point in arguing.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This contradicts paragraph 14, where he hands the narrator the sanding block and repeats his instructions. He expects the narrator to keep learning.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is too tired from his delivery to react strongly to anything.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The passage never mentions that he is tired. He notices the hidden board right away "as if it had called his name" (paragraph 10).

questions.solutionExplanation: Mr. Albescu "turned the board over in his hands for a long time" (paragraph 11) and then brings out his own first piece, made when "My teacher told me to wait, and I did not wait" (paragraph 12). He sees his younger self in the narrator's mistake. Instead of shouting, he uses the moment to teach, and he hands back the sanding block (paragraph 14), showing he still wants the narrator to learn.
questions.commonTrap: The "board can be repaired" choice tempts students who look for a practical reason. But Mr. Albescu answers the mistake with a story about his own first piece, which shows his calm comes from understanding, not from the damage being small.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of the poem?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The ocean is dangerous and should always be feared.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This is the speaker's view in lines 12–14, before the turn. The poem moves past this fear when the speaker discovers that "The sea had been holding me all along" (line 23).

choices.label: B
choices.text: Children must eventually learn to survive without their parents.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The father's hand does slide away (line 16), but his voice stays with her: "I hear him" (line 27). The poem is about trust, not about leaving parents behind.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Learning to trust, instead of struggling, can allow a person to be supported.
choices.explanation: Correct. The speaker "believed in fists, / in kicking, in the hard work of not sinking" (lines 5–6), but fighting only made the sea pull her down. When she stops fighting, she floats: "The sea had been holding me all along" (line 23). The last lines state the lesson: "some things will carry us best / when we stop trying to carry ourselves" (lines 30–31). Trusting, rather than struggling, lets her be supported.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hard work and determination are the keys to overcoming fear.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reverses the poem's lesson. What she calls "the hard work of not sinking" (line 6) is exactly what fails. She floats only when she stops fighting.

questions.solutionExplanation: The speaker "believed in fists, / in kicking, in the hard work of not sinking" (lines 5–6), but fighting only made the sea pull her down. When she stops fighting, she floats: "The sea had been holding me all along" (line 23). The last lines state the lesson: "some things will carry us best / when we stop trying to carry ourselves" (lines 30–31). Trusting, rather than struggling, lets her be supported.
questions.commonTrap: The choice about surviving without parents tempts students because the turn happens when the father lets go. But the final stanza brings his voice back as a guide. The lesson is about trusting what holds you up.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: The speaker's feelings change over the course of the poem. Match each group of lines with the feeling the speaker shows most strongly in those lines.

dnd.instruction: Move the correct feeling into each box. Not all feelings will be used.

pool.explanation: Belongs with lines 5 through 10. The speaker "thrashed like a fish dropped on a dock," "swallowed salt," and "grabbed his arm with both hands." She fights the water in fear.
Belongs with lines 16 through 22. The repeated "I did not go under. I did not" shows her surprise, and "the slow lift and settle of my breath" shows her new calm.
Belongs with lines 25 through 31. When troubles come, she chooses to "spread my arms" and "let the water rise," trusting what she learned.
Not used. The speaker is never disappointed in her father or the sea. Even when his hand slides away (line 16), the result is relief, not bitterness.
Not used. There is no contest or rival in the poem. The speaker's struggle is with her own fear.

dnd.solutionExplanation: Lines 5–10: she "thrashed like a fish dropped on a dock," "grabbed his arm with both hands," and fought the water, which shows panicked resistance. Lines 16–22: she discovers "I did not go under. I did not," and the noise fades until there is "only sky" and "the slow lift and settle of my breath," which shows surprised calm. Lines 25–31: facing new troubles, "I spread my arms. I let the water rise," which shows steady trust.

questions.solutionExplanation: Lines 5–10: she "thrashed like a fish dropped on a dock," "grabbed his arm with both hands," and fought the water, which shows panicked resistance. Lines 16–22: she discovers "I did not go under. I did not," and the noise fades until there is "only sky" and "the slow lift and settle of my breath," which shows surprised calm. Lines 25–31: facing new troubles, "I spread my arms. I let the water rise," which shows steady trust.
questions.commonTrap: Students sometimes put "bitter disappointment" with lines 16 through 22 because the father's hand slides away, which sounds like being abandoned. Read the next line: "I did not go under." The moment brings relief, not bitterness.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: How do lines 25–31 contribute to the poem?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They describe a second trip to Rockaway when the speaker was older.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reads "waves" and "water" literally. The waves are "a test, a slammed door, a night without sleep" (line 26), which are not ocean waves.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They apply the lesson the speaker learned in the ocean to difficulties in her present life.
choices.explanation: Correct. Lines 25–31 move from the beach to the speaker's present: "Now, when the world comes at me in waves, / a test, a slammed door, a night without sleep." The "waves" are now everyday troubles. She applies her father's advice, "Lie back. Let it hold you," to these new challenges, so the final stanza turns a childhood memory into a lesson for life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They show that the speaker has forgotten her father's advice.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reverses the stanza. The speaker says "I hear him" and repeats his words in line 27.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They suggest that the speaker still fights against her problems the way she once fought the water.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reverses her attitude. In line 28 she says, "I spread my arms. I let the water rise," which shows trust, not struggle.

questions.solutionExplanation: Lines 25–31 move from the beach to the speaker's present: "Now, when the world comes at me in waves, / a test, a slammed door, a night without sleep." The "waves" are now everyday troubles. She applies her father's advice, "Lie back. Let it hold you," to these new challenges, so the final stanza turns a childhood memory into a lesson for life.
questions.commonTrap: The "second trip" choice is tempting because the last stanza still uses ocean words like "waves" and "water." Line 26 shows those words are now figurative: the waves are "a test, a slammed door, a night without sleep."

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: In line 10, what does the phrase "as if my fear had weight and it could feel it" suggest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The speaker's panic seemed to be what pulled her under.
choices.explanation: Correct. Line 9 says that "every time I fought, the sea pulled down," and line 10 adds "as if my fear had weight and it could feel it." Fear has no real weight, so the image suggests that the speaker's panic was what dragged her down. Line 24 confirms this: "It was only my struggle it could not carry."

choices.label: B
choices.text: The speaker was carrying something heavy into the water.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reads "weight" literally. Nothing in the poem says she carries an object. The weight belongs to her fear.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ocean was angry with the speaker for being afraid.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The sea "could feel" her fear, but nothing says it was angry. The poem later shows the sea "had been holding me all along" (line 23).

choices.label: D
choices.text: The speaker's father could tell that she was frightened.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This misreads "it." The word refers to "the sea" in line 9, not to the father.

questions.solutionExplanation: Line 9 says that "every time I fought, the sea pulled down," and line 10 adds "as if my fear had weight and it could feel it." Fear has no real weight, so the image suggests that the speaker's panic was what dragged her down. Line 24 confirms this: "It was only my struggle it could not carry."
questions.commonTrap: Students who read "it could feel it" as giving the sea feelings may decide the sea is angry or hostile. The line is about cause and effect: the more she panicked, the more she sank.

questions.subject: ELA
questions.stem: Which line best supports the idea that the speaker's struggling, not the ocean itself, caused her to sink?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "bigger than all of Queens, something" (line 13)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This line explains why the speaker fears the ocean. It supports the opposite idea, that the ocean is too powerful to trust.

choices.label: B
choices.text: "swallowed salt, grabbed his arm with both hands," (line 8)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This line shows the speaker struggling, but it does not connect her struggle to her sinking.

choices.label: C
choices.text: "and the beach went small and far away," (line 19)
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This line describes what she hears and sees while floating. It says nothing about why she sank before.

choices.label: D
choices.text: "It was only my struggle it could not carry." (line 24)
